content: Exacerbation of tuberculosis (TB) signs and symptoms in patients with HIV-associated TB can occur shortly after the initiation of combination antiretroviral therapy (ART). Clinicians must perform a comprehensive evaluation to rule out other potential causes before diagnosing a paradoxical treatment reaction. In cases of paradoxical reactions, changes to antituberculosis or antiretroviral therapy are rarely required. However, if lymphadenopathy or other lesions are severe, it may be appropriate to continue antituberculosis therapy while administering short-term corticosteroids to suppress the heightened immune response. In a prospective study, six out of seven TB patients (86%) who initially had negative tuberculin skin test (TST) results demonstrated positive TST reactivity after starting combination ART, despite having low CD4+ T-cell counts. The size of the TST reactions post-ART ranged from 7 mm to 67 mm of induration. Clinicians should be aware of the potential public health and clinical implications of restored TST reactivity in individuals without active TB but who may have latent Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. Patients previously known to have negative TST results may benefit from repeat tuberculin testing if there is evidence of restored immune function following ART initiation, as TB preventive therapy is recommended for TST-positive HIV-infected individuals. When treating HIV-infected patients with antiretroviral agents, drug interactions between rifamycins (used for TB therapy) and antiretroviral drugs must be carefully considered. Commonly used antiretroviral drugs in the United States include protease inhibitors (such as saquinavir, indinavir, ritonavir, and nelfinavir) and non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) (such as nevirapine, delavirdine, and efavirenz). Protease inhibitors and NNRTIs exhibit significant interactions with rifamycins (rifampin, rifabutin, and rifapentine), primarily due to alterations in drug metabolism mediated by the hepatic cytochrome P450 (CYP450) enzyme system. Rifamycin-induced CYP450 enzyme induction reduces the blood levels of drugs metabolized by CYP450. For instance, when protease inhibitors are co-administered with rifampin (a potent CYP450 inducer), the blood concentrations of protease inhibitors decrease significantly, likely diminishing their antiretroviral efficacy. Conversely, when ritonavir (a potent CYP450 inhibitor) is co-administered with rifabutin, the blood levels of rifabutin increase markedly, raising the risk of rifabutin toxicity. Among the rifamycins, rifampin is the most potent CYP450 inducer, rifabutin has substantially less inducing activity, and rifapentine exhibits intermediate inducing activity. The four currently approved protease inhibitors, along with amprenavir (an investigational agent in Phase III clinical trials), are all inhibitors of CYP450 to varying degrees. Ritonavir is the most potent CYP450 inhibitor, followed by amprenavir, indinavir, and nelfinavir (which have approximately equal potencies), and saquinavir (the least potent). The effects of co-administering rifamycins and protease inhibitors have been evaluated in limited pharmacokinetic studies. The three approved NNRTIs have diverse effects on CYP450: nevirapine acts as an inducer, delavirdine as an inhibitor, and efavirenz as both an inducer and an inhibitor. The effects of co-administering rifamycins and NNRTIs have also been studied in pharmacokinetic evaluations or predicted based on their known potential to induce or inhibit CYP450.
